parameters.content:
### One job
The site saves the lead, then calls this webhook. This sends the email. That is all it does.

No queue, no schedule, no retry table. The site already knows the sheet title and the file link at the moment it saves the row, so it sends them in the request and nothing here has to look anything up.

**Expected body**
```json
{
  "email": "someone@company.com",
  "sheetTitle": "The Setup Sheet",
  "sheetDay": 1,
  "fileUrl": "https://.../sheet-setup.pdf"
}
```

### Both paths answer
The send has an error branch, and both branches end at a Respond node.

Without that, a failed send leaves the site waiting for a reply that never comes, and nobody finds out the email did not go.

200 means sent. 502 means it did not, and the site can log it.

nodes.name: Lead saved
nodes.notes: Called by the site straight after the lead row is written. If the row does not save, the site never calls this, so an email is never sent for a lead that does not exist.

=

nodes.name: Send the sheet
nodes.notes:
SMTP because it works on any provider. Swap for Gmail or Brevo if that is what this instance uses; nothing else changes.

A link, not an attachment: a link always points at the current file, so a corrected sheet reaches everybody, and mail filters treat a PDF from an unknown sender far worse than a link.

The three retries absorb a brief mail server blip so the site is not told a send failed when it merely stuttered.

parameters.responseBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ sent: false, error: 'mail_send_failed', message: String($json.error?.message || $json.error || 'unknown').slice(0, 300) }) }}

nodes.name: Respond not sent
nodes.notes: 502 and not 200. A 200 with an error in the body reads as success to the caller, so the site would log a delivered sheet that never left.
